title: Paper Rockets: Why Fins Keep Them Flying Straight
summary:
Can you build a rocket out of paper and launch it with a straw and a deep breath? This experiment shows why some rockets fly straight while others spin out of control.

Start by making rockets from paper and tape, then launch them by blowing into a straw. The challenge: can you make the rocket that flies the farthest? First try one with no fins. It may fly straight at first, but it spirals out of control, tumbling to the ground like a falling leaf.

Now add fins and launch again. The finned rocket should fly straight and travel farther, because the fins keep it stable and pointed in one direction. If it starts to turn, the fins help turn it back.

The same idea applies to everything that flies. Just as training wheels keep a bicycle steady, fins keep a flying object steady. Real rockets and missiles have triangular fins at their bases. The fins keep the rocket's center of pressure — where air resistance acts — behind its center of mass, where all its mass is concentrated.
why_it_matters: Trying a small experiment like this helps you test ideas with your own hands, just like scientists do when they solve real problems.

background_read: A rocket flies straight when it stays balanced and pointed in one direction, but the air can push it off course.
Fins are flat parts on the back of a flying object that help keep it steady, like training wheels keep a bicycle steady.
Real rockets use the same idea, with fins that keep the push of the air behind the rocket's balance point.
